chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Prayer of Fear. He said: 'The Imam stands up, and a group of his companions comes and stands behind him, while another group faces the enemy. The Imam prays one rak'ah with them, then stands up and they stand with him, remaining standing, and they pray the second rak'ah. Then some of them greet each other with salam, then they depart and stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. The Imam prays the second rak'ah with them, then the Imam sits, and they stand up and pray another rak'ah. Then he greets them with salam, and they depart with a single salam.'

He said: 'And in the Maghrib prayer it is the same: The Imam stands up, and a group comes and stands behind him, so he prays with them. Then he stands up and they stand up, and the Imam remains standing, and they pray the two rak'ahs, and they recite the tashahhud, and some of them greet each other with salam. Then they depart and stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand in the place of their companions behind the Imam. He prays one rak'ah with them, in which he recites. Then he sits and recites the tashahhud, and stands up, and they stand with him, and he prays another rak'ah with them. Then he sits, and they stand up and pray another rak'ah. Then he greets them with salam.'
ai.seo_question: How is the Prayer of Fear performed when facing an enemy?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* provides a detailed juristic account of the two-group method for Salat al-Khawf, emphasizing the Imam's role in leading the first half while the second half stands ready for combat. It notably extends the ruling to Maghrib prayer, illustrating the flexibility of ritual prayer under duress, a key concept in Shia fiqh derived from the principle of removing hardship. The text underscores the balance between maintaining congregational unity and ensuring military vigilance, reflecting the practical application of Quranic concessions during warfare.
